inklXsig4po.one_line: Two tahajjud reminders: the prayer is divided between Allah and His servant, and the standing is an act of reverence that deserves the most time.
inklXsig4po.summary: On the twenty-first night the sheikh's short reminders between the rakaat continue a look at the prayer posture by posture. In the first he says every position of salah has an outward form and an inner meaning, and that the prayer is shared: half of it belongs to Allah and half to the worshipper. He grounds this in the hadith qudsi where Allah says He has divided the prayer between Himself and His servant and answers each verse of al-Fatiha in turn: praise, glorification, the shared pledge of worship and seeking help, and finally the servant's own request for guidance, which Allah grants. The better a person understands prayer this way, the more he puts into the part that is for Allah. He asks the congregation to be absorbed in the purpose of each movement while they perform it. In the second reminder he turns to the first movement, the standing. Citing the teaching that the best prayer is the one with the longest standing, he compares it to students rising when their teacher walks in: an act of reverence and respect that also shows they accept what they are about to be taught, since the standing is where Allah's guidance and rulings are recited. He calls it the most important part of the prayer and urges people to give it unhurried time.

hadith.gist: Allah says: I have divided the prayer between Myself and My servant into two halves, and My servant shall have what he asks. When he says 'All praise is for Allah' Allah says My servant has praised Me; at 'the Most Merciful' He says My servant has extolled Me; at 'Master of the Day of Judgment' He says My servant has glorified Me; at 'You alone we worship and You alone we ask for help' He says this is between Me and My servant; at 'Guide us to the straight path' He says this is for My servant and he shall have what he asked.
The best prayer is the one with the longest standing.

3khsYni1WuU.title: Ramadan 2026 Night 19: Difficult Questions
3khsYni1WuU.one_line: Three hard questions Allah poses in the Quran: what were you doing, where are My partners, and did you think you would not be tested?
3khsYni1WuU.summary: The Quran is full of questions, and some are meant to be hard so we prepare our answers now. Life itself, he argues, is answering questions, and Allah has handed us both the questions and the answers in advance. The catch is that these answers cannot be memorised; like the open-book method of the old scholars, who had students teach the book back, the deen is only mastered by understanding and living it, not by Googling. He takes three passages. In An-Naml, Allah asks those who rejected His signs without studying them what they were doing with their lives, and they are left speechless because only truth can be spoken that Day; he admits he has no answer of his own and can only hope not to be asked. In Al-Qasas, after reminding us that only Allah gives night and day, He asks where the partners are whom people loved, feared or obeyed like Him, including those who simply followed their desires, and demands their proof. In Al-Ankabut, He asks whether people thought they could say 'we believe' without being tested. Believers who expect protection from hardship misunderstand the equation: iman is a precious claim, words are free, and tests expose who is truthful. He asks people to prove their claim and pray for strength to carry their burdens.

outline.heading: Hold firm when others ease off
outline.gist: As the last ten nights approach many people relax; to be chosen by Allah you have to stand out by showing up, especially the young.

outline.heading: Difficult questions in the Quran
outline.gist: Some are painful to face honestly, some are asked on the Day of Judgment of the unprepared, some are complex; they are posed early to prepare us.

outline.heading: Life is answering questions
outline.gist: School, family and courts all ask hard questions; the Quran's are about what your life, time, wealth and choices were for, and whether your belief was genuine.

outline.heading: The answers are given, but they must be lived
outline.gist: Allah supplied the questions and answers in advance, yet saying the right answer is useless unless it became part of your identity; memorising for an exam does not work here.

outline.heading: Open book: how the scholars tested mastery
outline.gist: His courses are open-book because understanding is what counts; the old teachers had the student teach the book back and sent him to restudy if he could not explain it.

outline.heading: Mastered only by practice, not by Googling
outline.gist: This knowledge cannot be mastered without living it; reducing the deen to answers copied from a web page misses that.

outline.heading: Did you deny My signs without learning them?
outline.gist: On the Day of Judgment Allah asks those who rejected His signs at face value; when they deny it, He asks them to explain what they were doing with their lives instead.

outline.heading: A life story he cannot defend
outline.gist: He says he could not justify his own book of deeds; how would anyone account for their youth, working years, strength and old age?

outline.heading: Silenced: only truth can be spoken that Day
outline.gist: The decree falls on them that they can only speak the truth, and because of their wrongdoing they have nothing to say.

outline.heading: If He asks the detailed questions
outline.gist: Like a lawyer going through your documents, Allah could ask about each day, blessing and choice; he can only pray not to be asked and to be found worthy of mercy.

outline.heading: Who brings light and night but Allah?
outline.gist: Before the story of Qarun, Allah asks who could bring light if night never ended, or rest if day never ended.

outline.heading: Where are My partners?
outline.gist: Allah asks to see those whose laws people treated as equal to His and whom they loved or feared as much or more; claiming many gods conveniently loosens ethics.

outline.heading: Taking desire as a god
outline.gist: No religion worships desire, yet the Quran twice describes the person who always does what he feels over justice, righteousness or empathy as having made desire his god.

outline.heading: You alone we worship: a claim to establish
outline.gist: When we say it in al-Fatihah Allah says this is between Him and His servant; it has to be proven by a life, not just recited.

outline.heading: Bring your proof: the truth belongs to Allah
outline.gist: A witness is brought from every nation and people are told to produce their evidence; they realise with certainty that truth is Allah's alone and their inventions vanish.

outline.heading: Did people think they would be left to say 'we believe'?
outline.gist: A real question at the start of Al-Ankabut, addressed to every one of us, about claiming iman.

outline.heading: Iman is a heavy claim
outline.gist: The Bedouins who claimed iman were told they had only entered Islam; the people in Al-Ankabut claim the higher level of proven commitment.

outline.heading: Expecting a red carpet for believers
outline.gist: He once thought giving up haram would shield him from hardship; asking 'why is this happening to me' shows a misreading of the equation.

outline.heading: Every nation before was tested
outline.gist: Every people who made the claim was tried, and Allah will make clear who is truthful.

outline.heading: Truthful whatever it costs
outline.gist: The truthful put Allah first even if it costs wealth, health or life; Allah will also expose the liars.

outline.heading: Evildoers who think they got away with it
outline.gist: Those who steal or commit zina and see no lightning bolt think they have outrun Allah; that is terrible judgment.

outline.heading: A precious claim words cannot carry
outline.gist: Iman of convenience will be shaken; Allah does not need our belief, yet eternal bliss is built on the claim, and like saying 'I love you' it means nothing without behaviour.

outline.heading: Tests are promised: ask for a stronger back
outline.gist: Testing is a divine promise; ask for tests you can pass, like his teacher who asked Allah not to lift his burden but to strengthen his back to carry it.

TvJLo83Sih0.title: Ramadan 2026 Night 22: Sincerity
TvJLo83Sih0.one_line: Sincerity as the goal of the whole deen, a gift Allah grants rather than an achievement, purified by remembrance of the Hereafter.
TvJLo83Sih0.summary: He argues that sincerity is not one value or act of the heart among others but the goal everything in the deen aims at, and that no one can achieve it alone: you line everything up and Allah grants it or not. Surah Al-Ikhlas, the only surah whose name never appears in it, shows why: Allah is one, self-sufficient and beyond time, in a league of His own, so sincerity is simply tawhid seen from the other side. If only One matters, everyone else becomes background noise. In As-Saffat, everyone is repaid by their deeds except the mukhlasin, a passive form meaning those Allah made sincere, who receive far beyond what they did; Yusuf and Musa are described the same way. In Sad, Ibrahim, Ishaq and Ya'qub were purified 'with something pure', which he identifies as remembrance of the final abode. Keeping the Day of Judgment in view ends every inner debate about right and wrong, which is why he refuses to carry other people's moral choices for them, as Imam Malik once answered a man who travelled from Morocco with 'I do not know'. In Az-Zumar, the Prophet is told to make his religion sincere for Allah and answers that it is Allah alone he worships. He asks people to keep refining their motives and to ask Allah to make them sincere.

outline.heading: Sincerity: a theme found everywhere in the Quran
outline.gist: He added it this year because it is so pervasive; seeing the Quran through its themes makes its teaching easier to navigate.

outline.heading: Sincerity is the goal, and Allah grants it
outline.gist: It is not one value or act of the heart but what all rulings, values and tazkiyah aim for; you prepare the ground and Allah gives it, or gives less than hoped.

outline.heading: Al-Ikhlas: a surah whose name never appears in it
outline.gist: Unlike almost every other surah, the word ikhlas is absent from the surah named after it.

outline.heading: One and only: no one in the same league
outline.gist: Because Allah is one, self-sufficient and without equal, nobody can sit near Him in your heart or decisions; it is not a ranking with a number two.

outline.heading: Only the Quranic description of God holds together
outline.gist: Any other picture of a creator runs into logical and metaphysical problems; Allah is self-sustaining, untouched by time and without lineage.

outline.heading: Sincerity: the flip side of tawhid
outline.gist: If no one else is worth fearing, revering or pleasing, caring about popularity shows you have not grasped it; true sincerity turns everyone else into background noise.

outline.heading: The delights promised in paradise
outline.gist: Known provision, honour, couches facing one another, a pure drink with no headache or intoxication, and spouses: everything the human heart hopes for.

outline.heading: Repaid by deeds, except those Allah made sincere
outline.gist: Everyone gets what they did except the mukhlasin; the passive form means Allah made them sincere, proof that sincerity is too big for a human to reach alone.

outline.heading: Yusuf and Musa: chosen and shaped by Allah
outline.gist: Yusuf is called one of Allah's sincere servants after refusing the minister's wife, and Musa was raised under Allah's eye; so ask Allah to make you sincere rather than trying to manufacture it.

outline.heading: Rewarded far beyond their deeds
outline.gist: The exception is on the generous side: no one gets less than their deeds, and the sincere get far more.

outline.heading: Ibrahim, Ishaq and Ya'qub: people of good deeds and insight
outline.gist: 'Hands' here means many favours done for others, and 'vision' means clarity about why they did them.

outline.heading: Bi-khalisah: purified with something pure
outline.gist: Allah did not say He used a tool that generates sincerity but something pure in its essence, a precise wording that strengthens his thesis that sincerity is a gift.

outline.heading: The pure tool: remembrance of the final abode
outline.gist: What purified them was remembering the Day of Judgment and where people end up, something no disease of the heart can mix with.

outline.heading: Remembering the Day ends every inner debate
outline.gist: Asking what you want written in your book and what you will explain to Allah settles choices immediately.

outline.heading: People who want the imam to carry their choices
outline.gist: Many come wanting a scholar's approval for what they already think is wrong, about debts, harm done, lies or cheating; he refuses to carry it for them.

outline.heading: Imam Malik and the man from Morocco
outline.gist: A man who sold his house to travel to Madinah with a question was told 'I do not know'; scholars would not carry another's dilemma.

outline.heading: The only pure elixir
outline.gist: Fame, wealth and power count for nothing on that Day, which is why the Quran keeps repeating its scenes; committing to reflect on it is the key to being granted sincerity.

outline.heading: A heart attached to Him alone
outline.gist: You still work, care for family and serve the community, but only for Him; you love and care for people because He told you to, and such people are among the chosen.

outline.heading: Commanded to make the deen sincere for Him
outline.gist: In Az-Zumar the Prophet is told to worship Allah with a way of life kept clear of anyone else's pleasure or opinion.

outline.heading: Refine it: question your motives
outline.gist: You cannot make your deen sincere, only keep refining it: ask why someone's approval pleased you or their displeasure pushed you, then repent and try again.

outline.heading: First of the Muslims: strive to be the best
outline.gist: 'First' is a rank of piety, not of time, so we are commanded to try to be the best Muslim, while fearing the punishment of a great Day.

outline.heading: It is Allah alone I worship
outline.gist: Putting Allah's name first makes the sentence a constant: the Prophet answers the commands personally, Allah and only Allah do I serve.

outline.heading: Worship what you will: the true loss
outline.gist: Content with Allah, he leaves others free to choose; the real loss is losing yourself and your family on the Day of Judgment, which comes from not doing it for Him.

LBo1RmX1nbU.title: Ramadan 2026, Night 22: Second Night of Tahajjud
LBo1RmX1nbU.one_line: Reminders on not outsourcing reflection on the Quran to AI, and keys for the last ten nights: removing distraction and letting life open the text.
LBo1RmX1nbU.summary: The reminders between the rakaat on this night come from a guest speaker, built around a young man's advice to prepare a talk with ChatGPT. He calls this a contradiction: the Quran says it was sent down so that people reflect on its verses, and reflection needs real thinking, which a language model predicting the next word does not do. Revelation itself came gradually, tied to events and struggle, rather than being loaded at once, and reading summaries of it is like the old practice of drinking dissolved verses, present in the body but never taking root. He is not against technology: use it for work, then spend the saved time with the Quran, and measure Ramadan by connection rather than by pages finished. Even with little memorized, the night prayer works through repetition that turns into contemplation. In the second reminder he offers keys for the last ten nights: remove the distraction of phones, learn the core vocabulary, and notice how each hardship opens a different passage, from Sarah's glad tidings to a Paradise free of sadness. Hard hearts and sins block the connection, and leaving them behind in Ramadan restores it.

outline.heading: Interlude
Just use ChatGPT
outline.gist: A well-meaning young man's advice to prepare a talk with an AI tool because it gives the best reflection, which the speaker found self-contradictory.

outline.heading: Sent down so that they reflect
outline.gist: The Quran repeatedly describes itself as a blessed book revealed so that people ponder its verses.

outline.heading: Reflection needs real thinking
outline.gist: Reflection draws on critical thinking, working memory and the confidence that you can think something through; a language model only strings together the most probable next letters.

outline.heading: Revelation was not downloaded
outline.gist: Sent to the lowest heaven on Laylat al-Qadr, the Quran could have been placed straight into the Prophet's mind, yet it came down gradually, tied to events and struggle.

outline.heading: Summaries like dissolved ink
outline.gist: Feeding pages into an AI for a summary is like the old practice of dissolving written verses in water and drinking them: inside you, but never taking root or causing change.

outline.heading: Read: the first command
outline.gist: The first word revealed was the command to read, and that first message is being forgotten.

outline.heading: Use technology to free time for the Quran
outline.gist: This is not a rejection of technology like refusing calculators or denying the moon landing; use the tools for work so you can sit with the Quran yourself, especially in the last ten nights.

outline.heading: The month is more than numbers
outline.gist: We made Ramadan about pages and completions, but what we should gain is a connection to carry into the rest of the year.

outline.heading: Night prayer works with little memorized
outline.gist: Feeling unqualified because of language or recitation is no barrier: the night prayer of al-Muzzammil means repeating what little you know over and over, and that repetition leads to contemplation.

outline.heading: Interlude
The Criterion, not a tool that gets it wrong
outline.gist: A tool that admits it was wrong cannot tell truth from falsehood for you; that is the role of the Quran itself.

outline.heading: First key: a world built for distraction
outline.gist: Like Pavlov's dogs, we react to every buzz and notification and lose track of what we were thinking.

outline.heading: Removing distraction: paper mushaf and vocabulary
outline.gist: Pick up a paper mushaf with translation, pass it on to the next generation, and learn the frequent words that make up most of the Quran so the night prayers are understood.

outline.heading: Second key: each life opens different passages
outline.gist: Barriers differ for each person, and the difficulties met through life make different parts of the Quran speak directly to you.

outline.heading: Sarah's glad tidings for the childless
outline.gist: Someone who has been through failed rounds of fertility treatment reads Sarah's reaction to the news of a child in old age like no one else.

outline.heading: A parent who sees the harm coming
outline.gist: Like a parent watching a child ride without a helmet, a father in the prophets' stories knows better yet must watch his son; parents feel those passages differently.

outline.heading: A Paradise without sadness
outline.gist: Someone too depressed to leave bed longs for the verse where the people of Paradise thank Allah for removing their grief in a way the healthy may never feel.

outline.heading: A mountain would crumble
outline.gist: Had the Quran been sent on a mountain it would split from awe, so the question is how our hearts became harder than rock.

outline.heading: Sins as a barrier to the Quran
outline.gist: Touching on the purified, he suggests that what we have seen, done and said may be why we cannot connect with the Quran.

outline.heading: Why Ramadan restores the connection
outline.gist: In Ramadan we leave things behind, so the connection returns; guard what comes across your screens.

outline.heading: People of the Quran who find healing
outline.gist: A closing prayer to be people of the Quran who find in it healing, the meaning behind the word often translated as medicine.

outline.heading: Interlude
Outro

mbWA7IFdIVI.one_line: Dua as our side of a conversation Allah began, drawn from Al-Furqan 25:77 and the supplications of Ibrahim and Sulayman.
mbWA7IFdIVI.summary: He frames dua as the brain of every act of worship and as our reply to a conversation Allah started through the Quran, a book that never goes stale the way even great human literature does. He warns against treating dua as Aladdin's lamp, since faith built on getting wishes granted collapses the first time a request is refused. The closing verse of Al-Furqan says Allah would not care for us at all were it not for our dua; he defends this by asking listeners to take Allah's perspective: a vast universe made from nothing, a single welcoming planet, the gift of intellect, and still most people never turn to the One behind it. He then studies Ibrahim's words on leaving Babylon, disowned by his father: he asks not for victory or wealth but for sound judgment, to be joined with the righteous, a truthful tongue, forgiveness for his father, and a sound heart. Prophets praying for those who harmed them, including the Prophet at Uhud, show the same mercy. Sulayman and Yusuf, at the height of power, ask only for gratitude and to be counted among the righteous, proving humility lives in the heart. He urges people to ask, for the rest of Ramadan, for what really matters.

Dua as a building block inside every act of worship
outline.gist: Acts like salah are built from smaller pieces such as invocation, recitation and submission, and dua runs through all of them.

outline.heading: Dua is worship: speaking back to the One who spoke first
outline.gist: The hadith call dua worship and the brain of worship; without it rituals are mechanics. Allah opened the conversation with 604 pages.

outline.heading: The Quran: a conversation that never expires
outline.gist: Almost no book stays relevant for centuries; even Shakespeare is hard to justify teaching to teenagers today, while the Quran still guides after 1400 years.

outline.heading: Every word read, defended and practised
outline.gist: Unlike traditions that study only selected chapters, Muslims recite and live every word, and the Quran set out an ethically coherent framework the social sciences are only now approaching.

outline.heading: Dua is not Aladdin's lamp
outline.gist: Treating dua as a wish machine is materialistic; he has seen people embrace Islam over one answered dua, and that understanding can break faith when a dua is not answered.

outline.heading: Ya'ba': to care is to carry someone
outline.gist: The verse asks what your Lord would care for you without your dua; the root word means a burden, because caring for someone means carrying them in your thoughts and worry.

outline.heading: Without dua you are insignificant: see it from His side
outline.gist: This is not harsh once you try Allah's perspective: He made time and a universe measured in hundreds of millions of light years from nothing.

outline.heading: One welcoming planet and the gift of intellect
outline.gist: Out of 13 billion years and a hostile cosmos, we alone can reason and reflect on our existence, and even a basic life is an extraordinary gift.

outline.heading: Uninterested in the One who gave us everything
outline.gist: Most people never ask who is behind their life or thank Him; pain exists so that we can recognise sweetness and health at all.

outline.heading: Dua: opening your whole heart to Allah
outline.gist: After revelation and a final messenger people still do not speak to Him; dua means sharing fears, hopes, regrets and plans, and the verse ends with a warning to those who deny.

outline.heading: Ibrahim's dua: only the Lord of the worlds
outline.gist: He renders Ibrahim's words: the Lord who creates, guides, feeds, heals, gives death and life and forgives; then the requests, with two valid readings of a truthful tongue among later generations.

outline.heading: Hukm: asking for good judgment, not power
outline.gist: Said as Ibrahim walks out of Babylon; hukm here is sound judgment, the ability to choose rightly when temptation, relationships and fear of loss cloud the decision.

outline.heading: We ask for stuff; he asked for judgment in exile
outline.gist: People ask for degrees, spouses and houses; Ibrahim, expelled and disowned, did not ask for victory or revenge but to keep making choices that please Allah.

outline.heading: Join me with the righteous, and forgive my father
outline.gist: He wants simply to be let in with the righteous, to have a tongue that speaks the truth before Allah, and forgiveness for the father who threw him out.

outline.heading: The prophet who prayed for the people who struck him
outline.gist: The Prophet described an earlier prophet wiping blood from his face while asking Allah to forgive his people for they did not know.

outline.heading: Uhud: the Prophet refuses to curse his people
outline.gist: Wounded, having lost Hamza and many companions, he is asked to pray against Quraysh; the companions regret asking, and he prays for their guidance instead.

outline.heading: A sound heart on the Day nothing else counts
outline.gist: On a Day when wealth and children do not help, only a heart free of arrogance, envy, hatred, selfishness and shirk will matter.

outline.heading: Sulayman: a kingdom no one has had since
outline.gist: He rode the wind, ruled people, jinn, birds and insects, and was a prophet son of a prophet; there was nothing left in the world to wish for.

outline.heading: Sulayman's dua: gratitude and being counted among the righteous
outline.gist: He asks only to be able to thank Allah for what he and his parents were given, to use it to please Him, and by His mercy to be entered among the righteous.

outline.heading: Humility lives inside: Yusuf at the height of power
outline.gist: Some early Muslims and some of his teachers kept a poor appearance to stay humble, but Yusuf, given rule and knowledge, still asks to die Muslim and be joined with the righteous; wealth and status can sit with a humble heart.

outline.heading: Ask for what matters this Ramadan
outline.gist: The prophets mean these requests sincerely; for the rest of the month ask for good judgment, truthfulness, good ethics and a place among the righteous.

34:46.ar: ۞قُلۡ إِنَّمَآ أَعِظُكُم بِوَٰحِدَةٍۖ أَن تَقُومُواْ لِلَّهِ مَثۡنَىٰ وَفُرَٰدَىٰ ثُمَّ تَتَفَكَّرُواْۚ مَا بِصَاحِبِكُم مِّن جِنَّةٍۚ إِنۡ هُوَ إِلَّا نَذِيرࣱ لَّكُم بَيۡنَ يَدَيۡ عَذَابࣲ شَدِيدࣲ‏
34:46.en: Say (unto them, O Muhammad): I exhort you unto one thing only: that ye awake, for Allah's sake, by twos and singly, and then reflect: There is no madness in your comrade. He is naught else than a warner unto you in face of a terrific doom

35:27.ar: أَلَمۡ تَرَ أَنَّ ٱللَّهَ أَنزَلَ مِنَ ٱلسَّمَآءِ مَآءࣰ فَأَخۡرَجۡنَا بِهِۦ ثَمَرَٰتࣲ مُّخۡتَلِفًا أَلۡوَٰنُهَاۚ وَمِنَ ٱلۡجِبَالِ جُدَدُۢ بِيضࣱ وَحُمۡرࣱ مُّخۡتَلِفٌ أَلۡوَٰنُهَا وَغَرَابِيبُ سُودࣱ‏
35:27.en: Hast thou not seen that Allah causeth water to fall from the sky, and We produce therewith fruit of divers hues; and among the hills are streaks white and red, of divers hues, and (others) raven-black

35:28.ar: وَمِنَ ٱلنَّاسِ وَٱلدَّوَآبِّ وَٱلۡأَنۡعَٰمِ مُخۡتَلِفٌ أَلۡوَٰنُهُۥ كَذَٰلِكَۗ إِنَّمَا يَخۡشَى ٱللَّهَ مِنۡ عِبَادِهِ ٱلۡعُلَمَٰٓؤُاْۗ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ عَزِيزٌ غَفُورٌ
35:28.en: And of men and beasts and cattle, in like manner, divers hues? The erudite among His bondmen fear Allah alone. Lo! Allah is Mighty, Forgiving

36:13.ar: وَٱضۡرِبۡ لَهُم مَّثَلًا أَصۡحَٰبَ ٱلۡقَرۡيَةِ إِذۡ جَآءَهَا ٱلۡمُرۡسَلُونَ
36:13.en: Coin for them a similitude: The people of the city when those sent (from Allah) came unto them

36:14.ar: إِذۡ أَرۡسَلۡنَآ إِلَيۡهِمُ ٱثۡنَيۡنِ فَكَذَّبُوهُمَا فَعَزَّزۡنَا بِثَالِثࣲ فَقَالُوٓاْ إِنَّآ إِلَيۡكُم مُّرۡسَلُونَ
36:14.en: When We sent unto them twain, and they denied them both, so We reinforced them with a third, and they said: Lo! we have been sent unto you

36:15.ar: قَالُواْ مَآ أَنتُمۡ إِلَّا بَشَرࣱ مِّثۡلُنَا وَمَآ أَنزَلَ ٱلرَّحۡمَٰنُ مِن شَيۡءٍ إِنۡ أَنتُمۡ إِلَّا تَكۡذِبُونَ
36:15.en: They said: Ye are but mortals like unto us. The Beneficent hath naught revealed. Ye do but lie

36:16.ar: قَالُواْ رَبُّنَا يَعۡلَمُ إِنَّآ إِلَيۡكُمۡ لَمُرۡسَلُونَ
36:16.en: They answered: Our Lord knoweth that we are indeed sent unto you

36:17.en: And our duty is but plain conveyance (of the message)

36:18.ar: قَالُوٓاْ إِنَّا تَطَيَّرۡنَا بِكُمۡۖ لَئِن لَّمۡ تَنتَهُواْ لَنَرۡجُمَنَّكُمۡ وَلَيَمَسَّنَّكُم مِّنَّا عَذَابٌ أَلِيمࣱ‏
36:18.en: (The people of the city) said: We augur ill of you. If ye desist not, we shall surely stone you, and grievous torture will befall you at our hands

36:19.ar: قَالُواْ طَٰٓئِرُكُم مَّعَكُمۡ أَئِن ذُكِّرۡتُمۚ بَلۡ أَنتُمۡ قَوۡمࣱ مُّسۡرِفُونَ
36:19.en: They said: Your evil augury be with you! Is it because ye are reminded (of the truth)? Nay, but ye are froward folk

95:5.en: Then we reduced him to the lowest of the low

2:31.ar: وَعَلَّمَ ءَادَمَ ٱلۡأَسۡمَآءَ كُلَّهَا ثُمَّ عَرَضَهُمۡ عَلَى ٱلۡمَلَٰٓئِكَةِ فَقَالَ أَنۢبِـُٔونِي بِأَسۡمَآءِ هَٰٓؤُلَآءِ إِن كُنتُمۡ صَٰدِقِينَ
2:31.en: And He taught Adam all the names, then showed them to the angels, saying: Inform Me of the names of these, if ye are truthful

2:32.ar: قَالُواْ سُبۡحَٰنَكَ لَا عِلۡمَ لَنَآ إِلَّا مَا عَلَّمۡتَنَآۖ إِنَّكَ أَنتَ ٱلۡعَلِيمُ ٱلۡحَكِيمُ
2:32.en: They said: Be glorified! We have no knowledge saving that which Thou hast taught us. Lo! Thou, only Thou, art the Knower, the Wise

2:33.ar: قَالَ يَٰٓـَٔادَمُ أَنۢبِئۡهُم بِأَسۡمَآئِهِمۡۖ فَلَمَّآ أَنۢبَأَهُم بِأَسۡمَآئِهِمۡ قَالَ أَلَمۡ أَقُل لَّكُمۡ إِنِّيٓ أَعۡلَمُ غَيۡبَ ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلۡأَرۡضِ وَأَعۡلَمُ مَا تُبۡدُونَ وَمَا كُنتُمۡ تَكۡتُمُونَ
2:33.en: He said: O Adam! Inform them of their names, and when he had informed them of their names, He said: Did I not tell you that I know the secret of the heavens and the earth? And I know that which ye disclose and which ye hide

7:179.ar: وَلَقَدۡ ذَرَأۡنَا لِجَهَنَّمَ كَثِيرࣰ ا مِّنَ ٱلۡجِنِّ وَٱلۡإِنسِۖ لَهُمۡ قُلُوبࣱ لَّا يَفۡقَهُونَ بِهَا وَلَهُمۡ أَعۡيُنࣱ لَّا يُبۡصِرُونَ بِهَا وَلَهُمۡ ءَاذَانࣱ لَّا يَسۡمَعُونَ بِهَآۚ أُوْلَٰٓئِكَ كَٱلۡأَنۡعَٰمِ بَلۡ هُمۡ أَضَلُّۚ أُوْلَٰٓئِكَ هُمُ ٱلۡغَٰفِلُونَ
7:179.en: Already have We urged unto hell many of the jinn and humankind, having hearts wherewith they understand not, and having eyes wherewith they see not, and having ears wherewith they hear not. These are as the cattle - nay, but they are worse! These are the neglectful

6:76.ar: فَلَمَّا جَنَّ عَلَيۡهِ ٱلَّيۡلُ رَءَا كَوۡكَبࣰ اۖ قَالَ هَٰذَا رَبِّيۖ فَلَمَّآ أَفَلَ قَالَ لَآ أُحِبُّ ٱلۡأٓفِلِينَ
6:76.en: When the night grew dark upon him he beheld a star. He said: This is my Lord. But when it set, he said: I love not things that set

6:77.ar: فَلَمَّا رَءَا ٱلۡقَمَرَ بَازِغࣰ ا قَالَ هَٰذَا رَبِّيۖ فَلَمَّآ أَفَلَ قَالَ لَئِن لَّمۡ يَهۡدِنِي رَبِّي لَأَكُونَنَّ مِنَ ٱلۡقَوۡمِ ٱلضَّآلِّينَ
6:77.en: And when he saw the moon uprising, he exclaimed: This is my Lord. But when it set, he said: Unless my Lord guide me, I surely shall become one of the folk who are astray

6:78.ar: فَلَمَّا رَءَا ٱلشَّمۡسَ بَازِغَةࣰ قَالَ هَٰذَا رَبِّي هَٰذَآ أَكۡبَرُۖ فَلَمَّآ أَفَلَتۡ قَالَ يَٰقَوۡمِ إِنِّي بَرِيٓءࣱ مِّمَّا تُشۡرِكُونَ
6:78.en: And when he saw the sun uprising, he cried: This is my Lord! This is greater! And when it set he exclaimed: O my people! Lo! I am free from all that ye associate (with Him)

6:79.ar: إِنِّي وَجَّهۡتُ وَجۡهِيَ لِلَّذِي فَطَرَ ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلۡأَرۡضَ حَنِيفࣰ اۖ وَمَآ أَنَا۠ مِنَ ٱلۡمُشۡرِكِينَ
6:79.en: Lo! I have turned my face toward Him Who created the heavens and the earth, as one by nature upright, and I am not of the idolaters

17:90.ar: وَقَالُواْ لَن نُّؤۡمِنَ لَكَ حَتَّىٰ تَفۡجُرَ لَنَا مِنَ ٱلۡأَرۡضِ يَنۢبُوعًا
17:90.en: And they say: We will not put faith in thee till thou cause a spring to gush forth from the earth for us

17:91.ar: أَوۡ تَكُونَ لَكَ جَنَّةࣱ مِّن نَّخِيلࣲ وَعِنَبࣲ فَتُفَجِّرَ ٱلۡأَنۡهَٰرَ خِلَٰلَهَا تَفۡجِيرًا
17:91.en: Or thou have a garden of date-palms and grapes, and cause rivers to gush forth therein abundantly

17:92.ar: أَوۡ تُسۡقِطَ ٱلسَّمَآءَ كَمَا زَعَمۡتَ عَلَيۡنَا كِسَفًا أَوۡ تَأۡتِيَ بِٱللَّهِ وَٱلۡمَلَٰٓئِكَةِ قَبِيلًا
17:92.en: Or thou cause the heaven to fall upon us piecemeal, as thou hast pretended, or bring Allah and the angels as a warrant

17:93.ar: أَوۡ يَكُونَ لَكَ بَيۡتࣱ مِّن زُخۡرُفٍ أَوۡ تَرۡقَىٰ فِي ٱلسَّمَآءِ وَلَن نُّؤۡمِنَ لِرُقِيِّكَ حَتَّىٰ تُنَزِّلَ عَلَيۡنَا كِتَٰبࣰ ا نَّقۡرَؤُهُۥۗ قُلۡ سُبۡحَانَ رَبِّي هَلۡ كُنتُ إِلَّا بَشَرࣰ ا رَّسُولࣰ ا
17:93.en: Or thou have a house of gold; or thou ascend up into heaven, and even then we will put no faith in thine ascension till thou bring down for us a book that we can read. Say (O Muhammad): My Lord be Glorified! Am I aught save a mortal messenger

97:3.ar: لَيۡلَةُ ٱلۡقَدۡرِ خَيۡرࣱ مِّنۡ أَلۡفِ شَهۡرࣲ‏
97:3.en: The Night of Power is better than a thousand months

LENwUQAXW9I.speaker_note: single speaker in the sheikh's Ramadan nightly Quranic Themes series; refers to the tazkiyah sessions he ran and his village childhood
LENwUQAXW9I.title: Ramadan 2026 Night 21: Using Our Intellectual Faculties
LENwUQAXW9I.one_line: The intellect makes us accountable; Saba, Fatir and Ya-Sin call us to contemplate, study creation and answer arguments with reason, on the first of the last ten nights.
LENwUQAXW9I.summary: Opening the last ten nights, he explains that Laylat al-Qadr celebrates the Quran and is hidden so believers prove themselves by committing to all ten. The theme is the intellect: the capacity to reason and reflect that set Adam apart before the angels and is the reason humans are held accountable, while leaving it unused puts a person below livestock. In Saba, Allah gives one piece of advice: stand for Him, alone or with others, and think deeply until you conclude the Messenger is neither mad nor inventing. Ibrahim and the Prophet both reached prophethood through such reflection, the latter in long seclusion at Hira until Jibril answered him. Signs mean nothing without a mind that contemplates, and he found his own students had never actually practised it, so he urges a daily habit. In Fatir, the variety of crops, rocks, people and animals leads to the statement that only the knowledgeable truly fear Allah, which he reads as scholars of the cosmos: the more you understand the eye, the cell or the stars, the deeper the awe. In Ya-Sin, a town answers its messengers' logic with talk of bad omens and threats, whereas Islam prevailed as the strongest idea, without physical miracles. He closes urging full effort in the last ten nights.

outline.heading: The best nights of the year
outline.gist: Many scholars concluded that the best ten days are the first of Dhul Hijjah and the best ten nights the last of Ramadan.

outline.heading: Laylat al-Qadr: celebrating the Quran, hidden to test commitment
outline.gist: The night honours the revelation this ummah must preserve in words and meaning; we celebrate by drawing close to Allah, and it is hidden so we commit to all ten nights.

outline.heading: The intellect: what makes us human and accountable
outline.gist: Our faculties of comprehension and reasoning separate us from every other creature and are why Allah holds us responsible, giving us the potential for the highest and the lowest.

outline.heading: Adam's intellect amazes the angels
outline.gist: Given names, Adam began to build sentences and express opinions, something the angels had never seen.

outline.heading: An unused intellect: worse than livestock
outline.gist: Animals cannot choose to grow their minds, so people who leave their faculties idle are described as more astray than cattle; knowledge and skill expand our capacity.

outline.heading: One piece of advice: stand for Allah and reflect
outline.gist: Allah tells the Prophet to give a single counsel: stand for Allah in pairs or alone, then think deeply about whether the Messenger is mad; he is only a warner.

outline.heading: Ibrahim questioned what people worshipped
outline.gist: Before prophethood Ibrahim went around asking why people worshipped the moon, sun and stars and what evidence they had.

outline.heading: Hira: seclusion with nothing but thought
outline.gist: The Prophet spent nights at a time in a cave with no books, company or distraction, visited only by Khadijah with food, simply contemplating.

outline.heading: What he reflected on until revelation answered
outline.gist: From a cave overlooking the Ka'bah and the horizon, now spoiled by graffiti, he weighed life's purpose and his people's path, until on a night like these Jibril came filling the horizon.

outline.heading: Signs mean nothing without a mind
outline.gist: Last night's theme of divine signs needs this one: signs do nothing for a monkey that takes bananas for granted.

outline.heading: Contemplation as a daily act of worship
outline.gist: In his tazkiyah sessions students nodded at 'reflect' for months without ever doing it; put the phone down, sit by a window or walk and think, as the Prophet's seclusion did.

outline.heading: Think it through and conclude
outline.gist: Allah asks for only one thing: dedicate yourself, reflect, and reach the conclusion that the Messenger came with the truth.

outline.heading: Deep acceptance changes behaviour
outline.gist: Conviction reached through contemplation goes below the surface and changes conduct; the night sky was the Prophet's screen, and the Quran helps those less able to reason it out.

outline.heading: Rain and the variety of kinds
outline.gist: Water brings fruits of different alwan, which here means kinds and species, not only colours; mountains have white, red and black rock.

outline.heading: Many sciences in two verses
outline.gist: People, animals and livestock are listed too, touching botany, geology, anthropology and more, ending with the statement that only the knowledgeable truly fear Allah.

outline.heading: Which scholars? Readers of the cosmic text
outline.gist: The 'ulama here are those who study creation, not only texts; historically the title 'alim went to people who had studied botany, physics or astronomy alongside hadith.

outline.heading: Awe grows with understanding
outline.gist: Knowing how the eye's cells process colour, how a single cell governs itself, or what Saturn's rings are made of produces a deeper subhanallah than the starry sky he loved as a village child.

outline.heading: Barely scratching the surface
outline.gist: Finding a single new receptor on a cell would make a scientist famous for life, which shows how little of creation we understand.

outline.heading: Islam invites study of creation
outline.gist: Unlike a simplistic medieval image of a bearded God zapping things into being, the Quran presents Allah beyond time and space and tells us to study everything He made.

outline.heading: Switching off the mind for desire

yNMmrc32fSs.title: The Values of Islam: Perseverance and Gratitude (Sabr and Shukr)
yNMmrc32fSs.one_line: Gratitude is the core value and perseverance its fallback in hardship; together they stabilize a believer against both success and failure.
yNMmrc32fSs.summary: He presents gratitude and perseverance as one spectrum: gratitude is the value, and perseverance is what a believer shows when pain makes gratitude impossible. Building on the hadith that every affair of the believer is good, he argues Islam gives moral meaning to both ease and hardship, so it is neither ascetic nor merely celebratory. The two act as moderators of character: gratitude keeps success from going to one's head, and perseverance keeps failure from turning into despair, giving emotional equilibrium amid life's inevitable ups and downs. There is no neutral third state; feeling neither usually means one has lost sensitivity to blessings. He traces kufr to covering up a blessing and notes that despair of Allah's mercy is likewise tied to loss of faith. Real gratitude means using wealth, health and knowledge for Allah and for people, which logically returns more. Gratitude is taxed, since one must first repay the blessing, while perseverance is tax free. Entitlement destroys gratitude, as parents see with entitled children and as Surah Quraysh warns. He closes by rejecting survivor's guilt: compare yourself to no one, use what you have to help others, and trust Allah's wisdom.

Sll_uk2HOyU.title: The Values of Islam: Intellect and Seeking Knowledge ('Aql and Talab al-'Ilm)
Sll_uk2HOyU.one_line: Critical thinking is a value and lifelong learning its principle; Islam treats both as worship and forbids surrendering your mind to anyone.
Sll_uk2HOyU.summary: Opening the personal values in his Ramadan series, he reframes intellect and knowledge seeking as critical thinking and lifelong learning. Intellect is the condition of religious responsibility and the only way to grasp revelation, while ignorance is the root evil, which is why the pre-Islamic era was named after it and the first revealed command was an open-ended iqra', a word meaning to gather, reflect and learn from others, not merely to read. Knowledge without thinking produces blind followers, and thinking without knowledge is limited; Islam demands both and treats learning as a moral and spiritual pursuit rather than an academic one. He uses Adam being taught the names to show that articulation and connected thought are what make humans unique. Islam had no war between religion and science; its golden age was when jurists were also scientists, and scholars who never leave the masjid lose touch with people's lives. Those in power dislike critical thinkers and prefer people knowing just enough to keep the system running. He insists one reaches certainty in Allah through questioning, then submits out of earned trust, and must never hand one's mind to parents, groups or a sheikh. He invites his own students to object and question.

outline.heading: Ignorance as the root evil
outline.gist: The pre-Islamic era is named for the dominance of ignorance, and the Prophet brought its opposite, beginning with the command to read.

outline.heading: Iqra' without an object
outline.gist: The first verses command reading without saying what to read; iqra' means gathering, reflecting and learning from those before you, much as English uses reading figuratively.

outline.heading: Neither blind following nor unaided thinking
outline.gist: Knowledge without critical thinking makes people follow their forefathers blindly, and thinking without knowledge leaves them limited.

outline.heading: The virtue of seeking knowledge
outline.gist: After the image of a donkey carrying books, he lists hadith on the obligation and reward of seeking knowledge and explains that the prophets left knowledge, not wealth.

outline.heading: Adam taught the names: the gift of articulation
outline.gist: The first thing Allah did for humans was teach them to name and describe things, and Islam makes critical thinking an obligation one is accountable for.

outline.heading: No one followed without evidence
outline.gist: Even the Prophet brought evidence, the scholarly ethic is 'bring your proof', and all agree that ignorance is evil; the epistemology debate is left for another series.

outline.heading: Ignorance spoils whatever it touches
outline.gist: Wealth, power or youth combined with ignorance only produce greater evil; the Quran sends people to those firmly grounded in knowledge.

outline.heading: The angels and Adam's speech
outline.gist: The angels voiced their fears, admitted they knew only what they were taught, and submitted when Adam connected the names into meaningful speech.

outline.heading: The scholar-scientists of the golden age
outline.gist: Islam had no religion-versus-science struggle; it peaked when jurists were also physicians and astronomers, since revelation and creation share one source.

outline.heading: Those who truly revere Allah
outline.gist: The verse on scholars revering Allah sits among verses spanning many natural sciences, showing whom it means.

outline.heading: Why power dislikes critical thinkers
outline.gist: Governments prefer people with just enough knowledge to run the system and enough distraction not to question it; Islam obligates questioning.

outline.heading: Communal obligations of worldly knowledge
outline.gist: Not everyone must be an engineer or physician, but enough must be, and every university step is rewarded when seen as a religious pursuit.

outline.heading: Scholars confined to the masjid lose relevance
outline.gist: The early imams were merchants and professionals, which is why their jurisprudence addressed real lives.

outline.heading: Critical thinking protects the deen
outline.gist: Without it, a trusted teacher can say anything; one questions everything to reach Allah, then submits out of trust built by reason.

outline.heading: Give up your mind for no one
outline.gist: No parent, friend, boss or group deserves your freedom of thought, and followers are not excused on Judgment Day for having just followed.

outline.heading: Teachers inform, students decide
outline.gist: His role is to share information and reasons, not to control; he encourages objection in his circles because the ummah needs thinkers, not sheep.

outline.heading: How knowledge transformed the first Muslims
outline.gist: The Prophet turned an ignorant people into a nation that sanctified knowledge and saw critical thinking as an obligation.

30:20.ar: وَمِنۡ ءَايَٰتِهِۦٓ أَنۡ خَلَقَكُم مِّن تُرَابࣲ ثُمَّ إِذَآ أَنتُم بَشَرࣱ تَنتَشِرُونَ
30:20.en: And of His signs is this: He created you of dust, and behold you human beings, ranging widely

30:21.ar: وَمِنۡ ءَايَٰتِهِۦٓ أَنۡ خَلَقَ لَكُم مِّنۡ أَنفُسِكُمۡ أَزۡوَٰجࣰ ا لِّتَسۡكُنُوٓاْ إِلَيۡهَا وَجَعَلَ بَيۡنَكُم مَّوَدَّةࣰ وَرَحۡمَةًۚ إِنَّ فِي ذَٰلِكَ لَأٓيَٰتࣲ لِّقَوۡمࣲ يَتَفَكَّرُونَ
30:21.en: And of His signs is this: He created for you helpmeets from yourselves that ye might find rest in them, and He ordained between you love and mercy. Lo! herein indeed are portents for folk who reflect

30:22.ar: وَمِنۡ ءَايَٰتِهِۦ خَلۡقُ ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلۡأَرۡضِ وَٱخۡتِلَٰفُ أَلۡسِنَتِكُمۡ وَأَلۡوَٰنِكُمۡۚ إِنَّ فِي ذَٰلِكَ لَأٓيَٰتࣲ لِّلۡعَٰلِمِينَ
30:22.en: And of His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the difference of your languages and colours. Lo! herein indeed are portents for men of knowledge

30:23.ar: وَمِنۡ ءَايَٰتِهِۦ مَنَامُكُم بِٱلَّيۡلِ وَٱلنَّهَارِ وَٱبۡتِغَآؤُكُم مِّن فَضۡلِهِۦٓۚ إِنَّ فِي ذَٰلِكَ لَأٓيَٰتࣲ لِّقَوۡمࣲ يَسۡمَعُونَ
30:23.en: And of His signs is your slumber by night and by day, and your seeking of His bounty. Lo! herein indeed are portents for folk who heed

30:24.ar: وَمِنۡ ءَايَٰتِهِۦ يُرِيكُمُ ٱلۡبَرۡقَ خَوۡفࣰ ا وَطَمَعࣰ ا وَيُنَزِّلُ مِنَ ٱلسَّمَآءِ مَآءࣰ فَيُحۡيِۦ بِهِ ٱلۡأَرۡضَ بَعۡدَ مَوۡتِهَآۚ إِنَّ فِي ذَٰلِكَ لَأٓيَٰتࣲ لِّقَوۡمࣲ يَعۡقِلُونَ
30:24.en: And of His signs is this: He showeth you the lightning for a fear and for a hope, and sendeth down water from the sky, and thereby quickeneth the earth after her death. Lo! herein indeed are portents for folk who understand

30:25.ar: وَمِنۡ ءَايَٰتِهِۦٓ أَن تَقُومَ ٱلسَّمَآءُ وَٱلۡأَرۡضُ بِأَمۡرِهِۦۚ ثُمَّ إِذَا دَعَاكُمۡ دَعۡوَةࣰ مِّنَ ٱلۡأَرۡضِ إِذَآ أَنتُمۡ تَخۡرُجُونَ
30:25.en: And of His signs is this: The heavens and the earth stand fast by His command, and afterward, when He calleth you, lo! from the earth ye will emerge

31:31.ar: أَلَمۡ تَرَ أَنَّ ٱلۡفُلۡكَ تَجۡرِي فِي ٱلۡبَحۡرِ بِنِعۡمَتِ ٱللَّهِ لِيُرِيَكُم مِّنۡ ءَايَٰتِهِۦٓۚ إِنَّ فِي ذَٰلِكَ لَأٓيَٰتࣲ لِّكُلِّ صَبَّارࣲ شَكُورࣲ‏
31:31.en: Hast thou not seen how the ships glide on the sea by Allah's grace, that He may show you of His wonders? Lo! therein indeed are portents for every steadfast, grateful (heart)

31:32.ar: وَإِذَا غَشِيَهُم مَّوۡجࣱ كَٱلظُّلَلِ دَعَوُاْ ٱللَّهَ مُخۡلِصِينَ لَهُ ٱلدِّينَ فَلَمَّا نَجَّىٰهُمۡ إِلَى ٱلۡبَرِّ فَمِنۡهُم مُّقۡتَصِدࣱۚ وَمَا يَجۡحَدُ بِـَٔايَٰتِنَآ إِلَّا كُلُّ خَتَّارࣲ كَفُورࣲ‏
31:32.en: And if a wave enshroudeth them like awnings, they cry unto Allah, making their faith pure for Him only. But when He bringeth them safe to land, some of them compromise. None denieth Our signs save every traitor ingrate

32:26.ar: أَوَلَمۡ يَهۡدِ لَهُمۡ كَمۡ أَهۡلَكۡنَا مِن قَبۡلِهِم مِّنَ ٱلۡقُرُونِ يَمۡشُونَ فِي مَسَٰكِنِهِمۡۚ إِنَّ فِي ذَٰلِكَ لَأٓيَٰتٍۚ أَفَلَا يَسۡمَعُونَ
32:26.en: Is it not a guidance for them (to observe) how many generations We destroyed before them, amid whose dwelling places they do walk? Lo! therein verily are portents! Will they not then heed

32:27.ar: أَوَلَمۡ يَرَوۡاْ أَنَّا نَسُوقُ ٱلۡمَآءَ إِلَى ٱلۡأَرۡضِ ٱلۡجُرُزِ فَنُخۡرِجُ بِهِۦ زَرۡعࣰ ا تَأۡكُلُ مِنۡهُ أَنۡعَٰمُهُمۡ وَأَنفُسُهُمۡۚ أَفَلَا يُبۡصِرُونَ
32:27.en: Have they not seen how We lead the water to the barren land and therewith bring forth crops whereof their cattle eat, and they themselves? Will they not then see

62:2.ar: هُوَ ٱلَّذِي بَعَثَ فِي ٱلۡأُمِّيِّـۧنَ رَسُولࣰ ا مِّنۡهُمۡ يَتۡلُواْ عَلَيۡهِمۡ ءَايَٰتِهِۦ وَيُزَكِّيهِمۡ وَيُعَلِّمُهُمُ ٱلۡكِتَٰبَ وَٱلۡحِكۡمَةَ وَإِن كَانُواْ مِن قَبۡلُ لَفِي ضَلَٰلࣲ مُّبِينࣲ‏
62:2.en: He it is Who hath sent among the unlettered ones a messenger of their own, to recite unto them His revelations and to make them grow, and to teach them the Scripture and wisdom, though heretofore they were indeed in error manifest

B7gEy-jOdls.title: Ramadan 2026 Night 20: Divine Signs
B7gEy-jOdls.one_line: Build iman on the constant signs of Allah in creation, history and the self, through Ar-Rum, Luqman and As-Sajdah.
B7gEy-jOdls.summary: Divine signs are a major Quranic theme and the first thing prophets were sent to recite; they are 'recited' because, like written words, they never change. The Quran asks us to contemplate ordinary things everyone sees, not specialist science, and to think past the sign to the One who set it in motion, since people who contemplate without guidance end up worshipping the sun or the stars. His central argument is that iman must rest on constants: the universe, history and one's own inner life. Faith built on answered duas, on circumstances or on a favourite imam collapses when those change; the only person to build on is the Prophet. He then reads the 'and among His signs' verses of Ar-Rum: humans made from soil, spouses for tranquillity, love and mercy, diversity of tongues and colours, night and day, lightning and rain. In Luqman, ships float by His will, and people who call on Him sincerely in a storm grow lukewarm once ashore, lacking patience and gratitude. In As-Sajdah, we walk over the ruins of nations that once ruled, a reminder that we are temporary variables with no grounds for arrogance, while dead earth revived by rain points to Allah. Allah has worked on His side of the relationship; ours is to respond.

outline.heading: Counting the last ten nights
outline.gist: The first and second tens are fixed; the last ten are nine or ten nights depending on whether Ramadan has 29 or 30 days.

outline.heading: Interlude
Reciting His signs: why prophets were sent
outline.gist: The first task of every prophet is to recite Allah's signs, and they are 'recited' because, like the words of a book, they are always there and never change.

outline.heading: Everyday signs, not specialist knowledge
outline.gist: The Quran does not ask for reflection that needs a degree; faith rests on the simple things everyone sees and most people take for granted.

outline.heading: Contemplation without guidance ends in worshipping the sign
outline.gist: Those who marvelled at the stars, sun or mountains without guidance worshipped them.

outline.heading: Think bigger: the force behind the signs
outline.gist: The Quran tells us to look past each sign to the One who put it in motion; real contemplation of sunrise, seasons and running water steadily strengthens iman.

outline.heading: Ar-Rum's wedding verses and our relationship with His laws
outline.gist: The verses read at weddings everywhere describe our relationship with Allah's laws in creation, and the key to it is contemplation.

outline.heading: Iman built on answered duas collapses
outline.gist: If faith depends on getting what you ask for, it crumbles when Allah delays or answers differently; he has seen individuals and whole populations lose faith this way.

outline.heading: The constants: the universe, history and your own self
outline.gist: Observing creation, reading history and knowing your own psyche give a foundation that does not change until the Day you have prepared for.

outline.heading: Never build iman on a person
outline.gist: Imams fall into scandal and people's faith falls with them; he tells his students to keep him out of their iman and look only to the Prophet.

outline.heading: From mud to thinking, feeling human beings
outline.gist: We came from soil and will return to it; mud cannot speak, yet Allah made from it beings who reason, love and hold morals, and we treat that as a given.

outline.heading: Spouses for tranquillity, love and mercy
outline.gist: Each person is restless until completed by a spouse; the consistent male and female design across species is purposeful, not random.

outline.heading: The Quran speaks to the norm, not the exception
outline.gist: Rare cases in nature or life do not overturn the rule; the Quran addresses the norm and exceptions are handled individually with a scholar.

outline.heading: Diversity of tongues and colours
outline.gist: The creation of the heavens and earth and the variety of languages, races and cultures are signs for those with knowledge.

outline.heading: Night for sleep, day for work
outline.gist: We are built for this cycle, and those who work long night shifts for years pay for it in their health and happiness.

outline.heading: Lightning, rain and the call to rise
outline.gist: Lightning brings fear and hope of rain that revives dead earth, and the heavens and earth stand by His command until He calls us out of the ground.

outline.heading: Ships that float by His will
outline.gist: A floating city of metal is accepted without thought; if the physics changed slightly ships would sink and there would be nothing to do, which is a sign for the patient and grateful.

outline.heading: The sea shaped human history
outline.gist: Sea travel and trade let humanity communicate and develop, and today's wars are still fought over access to sea routes.

outline.heading: Sincere in the storm, lukewarm ashore
outline.gist: When waves rise like mountains people call on Allah with full sincerity; once safe they become merely moderate and pray yawning, hoping the imam finishes early.

outline.heading: No composure, no gratitude
outline.gist: Those who reject the signs lack patience, like a toddler whose world ends over dropped ice cream, and lack gratitude; remember how you were in the storm.

outline.heading: Middle-aged and iman still unsettled?
outline.gist: It troubles him when people reach middle age with weak iman, since the signs have never changed and all point to one Creator.

outline.heading: Allah worked on the relationship; now your side
outline.gist: Like a marriage, every relationship needs effort; Allah created, provided, sent guidance and rescued us repeatedly, so our dua is a response to a conversation He began.

outline.heading: Walking over the dwellings of destroyed nations
outline.gist: Places where prophets preached are now poor markets, and Roman arches near his village, where a king once ruled, sit behind a garbage dump.

outline.heading: We are variables: no room for arrogance
outline.gist: Nothing stays the same and we are here briefly, so we must build on the constants and cannot deny the constant One behind them.

outline.heading: Dead earth revived: find Allah by observing
outline.gist: Water driven to barren land brings crops for livestock and people; the cycle of death and life shows that Allah is found by observing His creation, which leads to submission.

outline.heading: Outro

36:54.ar: فَٱلۡيَوۡمَ لَا تُظۡلَمُ نَفۡسࣱ شَيۡـࣰٔ ا وَلَا تُجۡزَوۡنَ إِلَّا مَا كُنتُمۡ تَعۡمَلُونَ
36:54.en: This day no soul is wronged in aught; nor are ye requited aught save what ye used to do

36:55.ar: إِنَّ أَصۡحَٰبَ ٱلۡجَنَّةِ ٱلۡيَوۡمَ فِي شُغُلࣲ فَٰكِهُونَ
36:55.en: Lo! those who merit paradise this day are happily employed

36:56.ar: هُمۡ وَأَزۡوَٰجُهُمۡ فِي ظِلَٰلٍ عَلَى ٱلۡأَرَآئِكِ مُتَّكِـُٔونَ
36:56.en: They and their wives, in pleasant shade, on thrones reclining

36:57.ar: لَهُمۡ فِيهَا فَٰكِهَةࣱ وَلَهُم مَّا يَدَّعُونَ
36:57.en: Theirs the fruit (of their good deeds) and theirs (all) that they ask

36:58.ar: سَلَٰمࣱ قَوۡلࣰ ا مِّن رَّبࣲّ رَّحِيمࣲ‏
36:58.en: The word from a Merciful Lord (for them) is: Peace

36:59.en: But avaunt ye, O ye guilty, this day

36:60.ar: ۞أَلَمۡ أَعۡهَدۡ إِلَيۡكُمۡ يَٰبَنِيٓ ءَادَمَ أَن لَّا تَعۡبُدُواْ ٱلشَّيۡطَٰنَۖ إِنَّهُۥ لَكُمۡ عَدُوࣱّ مُّبِينࣱ‏
36:60.en: Did I not charge you, O ye sons of Adam, that ye worship not the devil - Lo! he is your open foe

36:61.en: But that ye worship Me? That was the right path

36:62.ar: وَلَقَدۡ أَضَلَّ مِنكُمۡ جِبِلࣰّ ا كَثِيرًاۖ أَفَلَمۡ تَكُونُواْ تَعۡقِلُونَ
36:62.en: Yet he hath led astray of you a great multitude. Had ye then no sense

36:63.en: This is hell which ye were promised (if ye followed him)

36:64.en: Burn therein this day for that ye disbelieved

36:65.ar: ٱلۡيَوۡمَ نَخۡتِمُ عَلَىٰٓ أَفۡوَٰهِهِمۡ وَتُكَلِّمُنَآ أَيۡدِيهِمۡ وَتَشۡهَدُ أَرۡجُلُهُم بِمَا كَانُواْ يَكۡسِبُونَ
36:65.en: This day We seal up their mouths, and their hands speak out to Us and their feet bear witness as to what they used to earn

36:66.ar: وَلَوۡ نَشَآءُ لَطَمَسۡنَا عَلَىٰٓ أَعۡيُنِهِمۡ فَٱسۡتَبَقُواْ ٱلصِّرَٰطَ فَأَنَّىٰ يُبۡصِرُونَ
36:66.en: And had We willed, We verily could have quenched their eyesight so that they should struggle for the way. Then how could they have seen

GFhmSBeQJA0.title: Tafseer of Surat Yasin, Part 6 (55-67)
GFhmSBeQJA0.one_line: Paradise as a busy, joyful life, loneliness in this one, Shaytan's sworn hatred of humanity, and limbs that testify on Judgment Day.
GFhmSBeQJA0.summary: He recaps the three barriers to a living heart: failing to reflect, selfish materialism and asking the wrong question. The people of paradise are busy with enjoyment, a word he uses to correct young Muslims who picture paradise as boring. What is removed there is death, disease and sorrow, not stimulation; Allah's creation is vast, and a changed perspective frees people from the petty concerns that consume us here, just as facing death does now. Paradise is shared with spouses, which leads him to the loneliness of the elderly in the West: patients who drive hours just to talk to him, and an elderly couple whose six children all lived far away, compared with village elders who have a mosque, neighbours and someone to argue with. His teacher said the best of paradise is access to Allah's knowledge. Turning to the criminals, Allah asks why anyone ends up there after being warned not to follow Shaytan, a sworn enemy who hates humanity, as do people who share his hatred. The straight path means every step is clean, and Shaytan works by flooding us with options. On that day mouths are sealed and limbs testify, exposing the intentions we hid. He closes with a reading that the final verses mean Allah could have removed our choice, but gave it to us.

outline.heading: The life of the heart as a purpose of the deen
outline.gist: The health of what is inside you is as important as physical health, and is a major theme in the books of spiritual wayfaring.

outline.heading: First barrier: failing to reflect
outline.gist: Not learning from what came before or what lies ahead blocks the heart.

outline.heading: Second barrier: selfish materialism

outline.heading: Third barrier: asking the wrong question
outline.gist: Asking when the Hour comes is superficial; someone certain of it prepares instead.

outline.gist: He recites the passage and notes where the noon and tanween are fully merged with no trace in the recitation.

outline.heading: No soul wronged, then the outcomes
outline.gist: After the single blast and fair judgment, Allah describes the two outcomes.

outline.heading: The people of paradise are busy with enjoyment
outline.gist: Shughul means being preoccupied, and fakihun links to fruit eaten purely for pleasure; the description is full of life.

outline.heading: Paradise is not boring
outline.gist: Many young Muslims imagine a dull paradise; what is removed is only death, disease and sorrow, not stimulation.

outline.heading: An infinite creation to explore
outline.gist: We are a small, simple part of creation; in paradise people are exposed to far more, having learned gratitude and perseverance here.

outline.heading: Choice makes us stewards
outline.gist: Unlike creatures on a fixed track, humans choose, so we are responsible for others; forgetting this has nearly fried the planet.

outline.heading: The vastness of paradise
outline.gist: Its gates are vast and even the lowest dweller holds many times the size of the earth.

outline.heading: A changed perspective: losing without sorrow
outline.gist: People still strive and may lose, but a heightened understanding removes the overreaction and sorrow.

outline.heading: Death puts things in perspective
outline.gist: Reflecting on death already makes petty quarrels with spouses and siblings fade; Allah will purge such pettiness before paradise.

outline.heading: A different kind of busy, with their spouses
outline.gist: The busyness is not labour, and no one is there alone.

outline.heading: The loneliness of the elderly
outline.gist: Being alone is healthy but loneliness is not; patients drive two hours to his clinic just to talk.

outline.heading: An elderly couple with six children far away
outline.gist: Visiting a lonely immigrant couple after he arrived in 2013 troubled him and his father, unlike village elders surrounded by mosque, family and neighbours.

outline.heading: Shade, couches and whatever they call for
outline.gist: The anxiety of the unknown is gone and every desire is met.

outline.heading: Access to Allah's knowledge
outline.gist: His teacher said the best thing in paradise is unlimited access to divine knowledge, and he shares the excitement of intellectual joy.

outline.heading: Peace, a word from a merciful Lord
outline.gist: No war, oppression, dispute or anyone trying to take what is yours.

outline.heading: Stand apart today, you criminals
outline.gist: Imtiyaz is standing out, and here it is standing out in the wrong direction.

outline.heading: Did I not take a covenant: Shaytan's sworn hatred
outline.gist: Allah pauses to ask why anyone ends up in the fire; Shaytan chose to hate humanity and vowed to prove it unworthy.

outline.heading: Ramadan without jinn devils, but with human ones
outline.gist: Devils among the jinn are chained but human devils keep working, and the jinn are weaker than them.

outline.heading: Those who hate humanity are on Shaytan's page
outline.gist: People who wish destruction, disunity and widening inequality act like Shaytan; we are one family descended from Adam.

outline.heading: Worship Me: a straight path where every step is clean
outline.gist: Linking to his weekday values series, he says the straight path means the means are as pure as the end and people are never means.

outline.heading: He misled mountains of people
outline.gist: Jibill evokes so many people they would stack up like a mountain.

outline.heading: Shaytan's catalogue of options
outline.gist: He has no control over you but floods you with ideas until the right choice is unlikely; learn to tell his whispers from good thoughts.

outline.heading: This is the fire you were promised
outline.gist: Enter it today for your ingratitude.

outline.heading: Mouths sealed, hands and feet testify
outline.gist: Allah lets everything else speak; the person even argues with his own skin.

outline.heading: The self testifies to hidden intentions
outline.gist: A bad assumption about Allah's attention leads to ruin; the corrupt intentions we never admitted will be exposed.

outline.heading: A living heart does not let itself reach that moment
outline.gist: Aware of its intentions now, it makes the right decisions beforehand.

outline.heading: Blinded and frozen in place at the bridge
outline.gist: If Allah willed, their eyes would be covered as they race to cross, or they would be transformed and rooted to the spot.

outline.heading: Another reading: hearts that go blind in this life
outline.gist: One scholar reads the verses as Allah being able to remove our insight to the straight path here; it is hearts, not eyes, that go blind.

outline.heading: We gave you choice
outline.gist: Allah could have made us beings without choice, but gave us the faculties to choose right, and people failed to use them.

gZu9uxqOF8E.title: The Values of Islam: Humility and Etiquette (Tawadu' and Adab)
gZu9uxqOF8E.one_line: Humility must rest on the truth that all people are equal, and adab must flow from real humility, or both become an ugly performance.
gZu9uxqOF8E.summary: He takes humility and adab, earlier treated as tazkiyah topics, and presents them as values that only work when they are real. Artificial humility is arrogance in disguise, and adab without humility is a performance that collapses the moment someone disagrees with you. Values must be consistent, not circumstantial, or they are mere preferences. Humility is not an inferiority complex but an accurate sense of self-value: all humans are made of the same clay, so no one is better or worse. If you must assume anything about people, assume they may be closer to Allah than you, which keeps you from wronging someone Allah loves. Judging one's own deeds good is Allah's domain, so a believer credits good done to him to others and thanks them, while seeing his own good as Allah's enabling. Excelling in a field does not make one a better person. Arrogance and vanity ruined the worst figures in the Quran. Adab should be the natural outcome of humble character, and lack of it can void deeds, as the verse on raising voices over the Prophet shows. He illustrates with stories of Imam Malik's training, the Prophet's manners at a door, and an elderly scholar he met as a teenager who served water to everyone.

outline.heading: Humility and adab as values and tazkiyah topics
outline.gist: These concepts were covered in his tazkiyah series; here they are treated as ethics, with adab called the master of character.

outline.heading: The condition: they must be real
outline.gist: Artificial humility backfires; declaring your own humility shows you see yourself above others.

outline.heading: Adab without humility is a performance
outline.gist: Politeness to your face that turns into insult when someone disagrees with you is the worst kind of character.

outline.heading: Values are consistent, preferences are circumstantial
outline.gist: Choosing whom to trade with is a preference, but empathy and humility must be shown regardless of how others behave.

outline.heading: Humility is accurate self-value, not inferiority
outline.gist: We are all made from the same earth, so no one is better or worse; a humble person neither overestimates nor underestimates himself.

outline.heading: Assume others are closer to Allah
outline.gist: Outside situations of safety and responsibility, the safe assumption is that others may be more beloved to Allah, so you never mistreat them.

outline.heading: Judging deeds is Allah's domain
outline.gist: See good from others and thank them, but see your own good as Allah working through you and leave its value for Him to judge.

outline.heading: Excelling in a field does not make you better
outline.gist: Islam never asks you to lie to yourself; skill in sport or academics is mostly gifts and circumstances, and Allah alone praises whom He wills.

outline.heading: Arrogance and vanity: the ruin of the worst
outline.gist: The most evil figures in the Quran failed to calibrate their self-value, and arrogance bars entry to Paradise.

outline.heading: Adab as the natural fruit of humility
outline.gist: Islam wants people to become naturally polite through understanding the world, not to mask rudeness with politeness.

outline.heading: Lack of adab voids deeds
outline.gist: Raising voices above the Prophet's makes deeds worthless, and a little adab is worth more than much knowledge.

outline.heading: Scholars on adab: Imam Malik's training
outline.gist: The whole deen is adab with Allah, His Messenger, the Quran and Muslims; Malik's mother sent him to learn manners before knowledge and a student spent most of twenty years learning his adab.

outline.heading: The Prophet at the door
outline.gist: He knocked and stood to the side so as not to see inside, a simple but meaningful act of manners.

outline.heading: The elderly scholar who served water
outline.gist: As a teenager he met an aged imam who spent his life offering water to people and refused to let others serve him.

outline.heading: The mask always falls
outline.gist: Repressed arrogance and disrespect eventually burst out at success or disagreement unless humility and adab are genuine.

outline.heading: Good manners as a part of prophethood
outline.gist: Humility needs long study and adab a lifetime; good demeanour is one of the parts of prophethood still open to everyone.

outline.heading: Outro

l7E2pQ49Sek.speaker: adnan
l7E2pQ49Sek.speaker_note: His annual end-of-Ramadan seven-part series; refers to teaching in Syria, his medical practice in Canada and his masjid courses
l7E2pQ49Sek.title: The Philosophy of Islamic Thought 1: Introduction to Understanding Ideologies
l7E2pQ49Sek.one_line: Why Muslims in the West must understand Islam as an ideology, and the framework of questions that defines any ideology.
l7E2pQ49Sek.summary: He opens a series on the philosophy of Islamic thought, arguing that Muslim youth in Western schools and universities face questions built on how the West understands ideologies, while they were taught Islam only as rules and basic beliefs. Philosophy, he says, is not to be feared: it asks what worldview makes the Quran a source of authority in the first place. Public opinion is born in academia before reaching government, media and the masses, so Muslims who want to influence causes like Palestine or the critique of usury must argue in academic language. He defines ideology as a coherent system of beliefs, values and ideas that shapes how people understand the world and guides action, insisting that deen means a way of life rather than a watered-down religion. Using Michael Freeden's framework, he walks through the questions the audience is asked to answer for Islam: what problem it solves, its picture of reality, its theory of human nature, its sources of knowledge and what it distrusts, its moral hierarchy, its mechanism of change, its ideal outcome, its internal tensions, and its historical context. Along the way he likens an ideology to a diagnosis and to an immune system, warns that tyranny destroys people's ability to think, explains why he rejects groups like ISIS at the level of their mechanism of change, and calls for honesty about Muslims' internal failings.

outline.heading: Opening
Why this topic: the questions Muslim youth face here
outline.gist: Students meet arguments framed by Western ideologies but learned Islam only as basics and rules, without a systematic way to articulate it.

outline.heading: What philosophy means
outline.gist: Not halal and haram or the evidence for them, but the worldview that makes the Quran your source of authority.

outline.heading: Do not demonize philosophy
outline.gist: Islam is a way of life and must have its philosophy of finance, society, the individual and ethics.

outline.heading: Public opinion is born in academia
outline.gist: Ideas move from dissertations to government, media and then the masses; the West's shift away from shared ethics began with liberal academics.

outline.heading: Muslim causes must be argued in academic language
outline.gist: Palestine or the critique of usury will change only through rigorous papers that survive peer scrutiny, the world's language of argument.

outline.heading: The burden of Muslims in the West
outline.gist: The West exports ideas to the world, so Muslims here must bring their philosophy to the table; influence is growing but not organized.

outline.heading: Sources for the series
outline.gist: Michael Freeden's and Andrew Heywood's works on ideology, plus Islamic sources including a classical response to the Greek philosophers.

outline.heading: Deen is a way of life, not 'religion'
outline.gist: The modern word religion is deliberately diluted; deen translates best as an ideology or way of life.

outline.heading: Defining ideology
outline.gist: A coherent, organized system of beliefs, values and ideas that shapes understanding and guides action; beliefs have evidence but not physical proof.

outline.heading: Why people need ideologies
outline.gist: Life never gives a time-out to ask who you are and why you are here; ideologies answer that and guide action.

outline.heading: Freeden's framework of questions
outline.gist: A set of questions that, once answered, defines any ideology; the audience answers them for Islam.

outline.heading: Question 1: which problem does it solve
outline.gist: Answer for Islam in your own words.

outline.heading: Students' sticky notes: everything is haram
outline.gist: Most grade seven and eight students wrote that everything is forbidden, showing how badly Islam had been explained to them.

outline.heading: Every ideology begins with a complaint about reality
outline.gist: Injustice, corrupted truth, lost freedom or chaos; what problem was the Prophet sent to change, answered as one coherent idea, not a list.

outline.heading: Ideology as diagnosis
outline.gist: Like a full cancer diagnosis before a treatment plan; in the Middle East explaining a diagnosis to patients is seen as weakness, showing how expectations differ.

outline.heading: Question 2: which picture of reality does it assume
outline.gist: Metaphysics: is the world material or moral, ordered or random, governed by law, struggle, divine will or chance, progressive or cyclical.

outline.heading: No one opts out of metaphysics
outline.gist: Atheism and agnosticism are answers too and shape choices and character; religion has wrongly been boxed into this one question.

outline.heading: Question 3: what is its theory of human nature
outline.gist: Good, corrupt or blank slate, rational or spiritual, free or determined; those who leave Islam rarely know what view of humans they are adopting.

outline.heading: The professor who denied free will
outline.gist: He asked why the professor spent a week trying to persuade someone without free will; change an ideology's anthropology and everything mutates.

outline.heading: Question 4: its sources of knowledge and authority
outline.gist: Reason, revelation, tradition, science, history or experience; without answers to these questions it is not an ideology.

outline.heading: What an ideology distrusts
outline.gist: The million-dollar question: liberalism, for example, is built on distrust of anyone holding power.

outline.heading: Ideology as an immune system
outline.gist: It defines what is a threat; Islam gives immunity in a sea of random ideas and AI-driven disinformation, which is why youth are warned off certain voices.

outline.heading: Learn your own faith first
outline.gist: If it does not make you more immune, leave it; learned properly, Islam is bulletproof, and it hurts to see people driven away by extremists and bad teaching.

outline.heading: Question 5: its core values and moral hierarchy
outline.gist: You are defined by your ranked values, not by the length of your beard or your hat.

outline.heading: Rulings are consequences; everyone ranks values
outline.gist: Ethical dilemmas force a ranking, and the record on Judgment Day shows which values you actually put first.

outline.heading: Never give up your freedom of thought
outline.gist: Tyranny in the Muslim world took away people's ability to think; they can take your wealth but not your freedom of belief.

outline.heading: Conflicts come from ranking values differently
outline.gist: No one lacks values; conflict arises when the top values differ.

outline.heading: Muslims cannot name their core values
outline.gist: Fifty Muslims give fifty-three answers on the fundamentals; Muslims share much with what the West claims to believe, though not with its practice.

outline.heading: Question 6: its suggested mechanism of change
outline.gist: How does it move from the problem it identified to a different reality.

outline.heading: Why he rejects groups like ISIS and the Taliban
outline.gist: Their answer to the mechanism of change is fundamentally different; philosophy is the code, and wrong code produces wrong outcomes.

outline.heading: Options for change: from philosophy to action
outline.gist: Education, revolution, legislation, moral reform, economics, spiritual awakening or governance: what exactly will you do on the ground.

outline.heading: Islamic history is human history

45ZWV9ynhlE.title: The Values of Islam: Strength and Forbearance (Quwwah and Hilm)
45ZWV9ynhlE.one_line: Muslims must seek strength in every field to protect the truth, and restrain it with forbearance so it never turns into oppression.
45ZWV9ynhlE.summary: He pairs strength and forbearance as complementary values that together balance character. Strength means psychological, moral, spiritual, political and physical strength, commanded in the Quran and praised in the hadith of the strong believer. He contrasts prophets whose people dismissed them as powerless with Sulayman, whose strength brought the Queen of Sheba and her people to Islam. The world still runs on the law of the jungle, where laws bind only the weak, so truth needs strength to survive. Weakness, as the hadith of nations feasting on the ummah explains, comes from loving this life and fearing death, which ranks survival above one's values and makes people sell out under pressure. Strength protects against moral collapse, while hilm, the refusal to be provoked, protects strength from becoming corruption, as parents easily abuse power over children. Islam wants people to bring out their inner strength and then control it. He illustrates hilm with a man who insulted a judge's mother, Ali Zayn al-Abidin freeing the servant who caused his child's death, the Prophet's response to a Bedouin who choked him after Hunayn, and the Prophet's physical strength in wrestling. He urges Muslims to become strong in every domain, pointing to how the powerful behave without moral restraint.

outline.gist: If living is your top priority, every value below it will be sold under threat; strength guards against moral collapse.

outline.gist: Strength without forbearance becomes destructive, as parents can abuse power over children; Arabs prized hilm and Ibrahim was described with it.

outline.gist: Islam does not want timid sheep; release the inner strength and control it so it harms no one.

outline.heading: Ali Zayn al-Abidin and the servant
outline.gist: When a servant's accident killed his child, he applied the verse on restraining anger and pardoning, and freed her.

outline.heading: Al-Ashajj of Abd al-Qays
outline.gist: The Prophet praised his forbearance and deliberateness, and he thanked Allah for creating him with traits Allah loves.

outline.heading: The Bedouin who choked the Prophet after Hunayn
outline.gist: Exhausted and taking nothing for himself, the Prophet was seized and choked yet calmed his companions and gave the man what he wanted.

outline.heading: Never angry for himself
outline.gist: He never retaliated for his own sake, but his anger could not be contained when truth was violated until justice was restored.

outline.heading: The Prophet's physical strength
outline.gist: His forbearance came from strength: Fatimah's description of his build in his fifties and his wrestling a strong man three times when a tribe demanded it.

outline.heading: Confronting the mockers at the Ka'bah
outline.gist: When Quraysh's insults went too far, he warned them face to face and they fell silent, showing patience was not fear.

outline.heading: The strong one masters his temper; seek strength
outline.gist: True strength is restraining one's temper, and Muslims must seek academic, physical, financial, social and political strength because a weak Muslim helps no one.

outline.heading: Strength without a moral compass
outline.gist: The behaviour of the powerful today shows human depravity without values, which is why the righteous need both strength and forbearance.
